newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: ASEAN meets over Cambodia membership.
newsitem.headline: ASEAN meets over Cambodia membership.

text.p: The Association of South East Asian Nations (ASEAN) began an emergency meeting on Thursday to discuss strife-torn Cambodia, whose impending membership in the group hangs in the balance.

"Everything related to Cambodia will be discussed including membership (in ASEAN)...and including life and properties (in Cambodia)," Philippine Foreign Minister Domingo Siazon told reporters just before the meeting started.
ASEAN was to admit Cambodia, Burma and Laos as final members at its annual meeting at the end of this month in Kuala Lumpur.
But Cambodian Second Prime Minister Hun Sen's bloody power grab over the weekend has cast doubt over those plans.

At least 58 people have died and up to 200 have been wounded in clashes between forces loyal to Hun Sen and those of his rival, First Prime Minister Norodom Ranariddh, according to preliminary estimates. One of the victims was a senior Ranariddh official who was shot dead.

Malaysian Foreign Minister Abdullah Ahmad Badawi told reporters late on Monday there should be no confusion about the decision to admit Cambodia into ASEAN and the timing of its entry. "We will be very practical and pragmatic about it," he said.
Abdullah did not reiterate Malaysia's oft-stated position that the three new members should be inducted at the July meeting, which will celebrate the 30th anniversary of the founding of ASEAN.
Malaysia is this year's chairman of ASEAN, which also includes Indonesia, Brunei, the Philippines, Singapore, Thailand and Vietnam.

ASEAN heads of state at an informal summit in Jakarta last December decided to admit the final three members as a group some time this year. They left it to their foreign ministers to fix the exact date.
The foreign ministers decided at a meeting in Kuala Lumpur on May 31 to admit them at the July meeting.

At the time, the decision was heavily criticised by Western governments and human rights groups who were seeking to isolate Burma over its poor human rights record and crackdown on a democracy movement led by 1991 Nobel Peace laureate Aung San Suu Kyi.

ASEAN was likely to put off Cambodia's membership because the group would not want to give "de facto recognition to Hun Sen's coup d'etat", said Abdul Razak Baginda, executive director of the Malaysian Strategic Research Centre.
Analysts said one key question for the foreign ministers was who would represent Cambodia at the July meeting and sign the various membership documents.

They would also have to decide whether to defer Cambodia's membership but accept Burma and Laos or postpone the entry of all three, possibly to the end of the year when the next ASEAN informal summit is held in Kuala Lumpur.
U.S. State Department spokesman Nicholas Burns said Washington had "given some advice" to ASEAN for its Thursday meeting.
He refused to say specifically what that advice was.

"It's very important at a time like this when there's chaos in Cambodia, when they're on the verge of a civil war, when fighting is occurring throughout the country between forces of the two major political parties, for countries that have an interest in Cambodia to speak out about what is acceptable and what is not acceptable," he said.
